lead: A tendon is jacked to a chosen force, but that force does not stay. The jacking force P0 is measured at the jack. The concrete shortens, the duct rubs, the anchor beds in, and time brings creep, shrinkage and relaxation. Each effect removes a small part of P0. The remaining force is the effective prestress P_eff. Design for service uses P_eff, not P0. The idea matters on every post-tensioned slab, bridge girder and water tank where the designer must know the force that actually presses the concrete.

blocks.text: A loss is a reduction in tendon force after jacking. Immediate losses happen during transfer or stressing. Time-dependent losses grow over months. The total loss ΔP is the sum of all force losses, in kN.
The effective prestress is:
P_eff = P0 − ΔP_es − ΔP_fr − ΔP_slip − ΔP_cr − ΔP_sh − ΔP_rel
blocks.where: P_eff is the effective prestress force after all losses (kN); P0 is the jacking force (kN); ΔP_es is elastic shortening loss, ΔP_fr is friction loss, ΔP_slip is anchorage slip loss, ΔP_cr is creep loss, ΔP_sh is shrinkage loss and ΔP_rel is relaxation loss, all in kN.

blocks.text: For a preliminary estimate, take each loss as a percentage of P0 and add the percentages. That estimate assumes each loss is independent of the others. It is not exact, because losses interact. State the assumption when you use it.
Elastic shortening happens when the tendon compresses the concrete. In a pre-tensioned member the concrete shortens at transfer. The tendon shortens with it. The stress loss is
Δf<sub>p,es</sub> = (E<sub>s</sub> / E<sub>c</sub>) f<sub>cp</sub>
blocks.where: Δf<sub>p,es</sub> is tendon stress loss (N/mm²); E<sub>s</sub> is steel modulus (N/mm²); E<sub>c</sub> is concrete modulus (N/mm²); f<sub>cp</sub> is concrete compressive stress at tendon level (N/mm²). Force loss ΔP<sub>es</sub> = A<sub>ps</sub> Δf<sub>p,es</sub> / 1000 (kN), with A<sub>ps</sub> the tendon area (mm²) and Δf<sub>p,es</sub> in N/mm².

blocks.text: In a post-tensioned member jacked one tendon at a time, earlier tendons lose force when later tendons compress the concrete. Jack all tendons together and this loss is small.
Friction in a post-tensioned duct has two parts. Curvature friction depends on the angle change. Wobble friction depends on length. The force at distance x from the jack is
P<sub>x</sub> = P0 e<sup>−μα − kx</sup>
blocks.where: P<sub>x</sub> is tendon force at x (kN); P0 is jacking force (kN); μ is curvature friction coefficient (dimensionless); α is total angle change from jack to x (radians); k is wobble coefficient (per metre); x is distance from jack (m); e is 2.718.

blocks.text: Use radians in μα. A 5° angle is 0.087 rad. The loss is P0 − P<sub>x</sub>.

At the anchor, the wedge or plate beds into the concrete by a slip δ. For a simple estimate, ignore friction and take the whole tendon of length L to shorten uniformly by δ. The stress loss along the tendon is
Δf<sub>p,slip</sub> = (E<sub>s</sub> δ) / L
blocks.where: Δf<sub>p,slip</sub> is tendon stress loss (N/mm²); E<sub>s</sub> is steel modulus (N/mm²); δ is anchorage slip (mm); L is full tendon length (mm); friction is ignored. Force loss ΔP<sub>slip</sub> = A<sub>ps</sub> Δf<sub>p,slip</sub> / 1000 (kN), with A<sub>ps</sub> in mm² and Δf<sub>p,slip</sub> in N/mm².

blocks.text: With friction, the slip is absorbed over a shorter affected length l<sub>s</sub> found from the friction slope. The tendon strain varies from a maximum at the anchor to zero at the end of l<sub>s</sub>. The loss at the anchor is about
Δf<sub>p,slip</sub> = (2 E<sub>s</sub> δ) / l<sub>s</sub>
blocks.where: Δf<sub>p,slip</sub> is tendon stress loss at the anchor (N/mm²); E<sub>s</sub> is steel modulus (N/mm²); δ is anchorage slip (mm); l<sub>s</sub> is affected length over which slip is absorbed (mm). The loss falls linearly to zero at the end of l<sub>s</sub>. The simple estimate with L understates the anchor loss when friction is significant.

blocks.text: Creep is slow shortening of concrete under sustained compression. The tendon follows the concrete and loses stress:
Δf<sub>p,cr</sub> = (E<sub>s</sub> / E<sub>c</sub>) φ f<sub>cp</sub>
blocks.where: Δf<sub>p,cr</sub> is creep stress loss (N/mm²); φ is creep coefficient (dimensionless); other symbols as before.

blocks.text: Shrinkage is drying shrinkage of concrete. It pulls the tendon inward. The stress loss is
Δf<sub>p,sh</sub> = ε<sub>sh</sub> E<sub>s</sub>
blocks.where: Δf<sub>p,sh</sub> is shrinkage stress loss (N/mm²); ε<sub>sh</sub> is shrinkage strain (dimensionless); E<sub>s</sub> is steel modulus (N/mm²).

blocks.text: Relaxation is loss of stress in steel held at constant strain. It depends on the steel type and initial stress. Low-relaxation strand loses less than ordinary stress-relieved strand. Use the manufacturer's value or the code table. A typical low-relaxation value is about 2% of the initial prestress.
Add all force losses to get P_eff. Check service stresses with P_eff, as in 6.4. Design checks that use effective force come in 6.6.

figure.caption: The effective force falls from 100% at jacking by an immediate step to about 91%, then time-dependent losses bring it to about 80% after twelve months.

spec.aria: The prestress force starts at 100 percent at jacking and drops vertically to about 91 percent at transfer, then falls gradually to 80 percent after twelve months as time-dependent losses accumulate.

examples.question: A post-tensioned beam is jacked to P0 = 1000 kN. For a preliminary estimate take friction 4%, anchorage slip 3%, elastic shortening 2%, creep 6%, shrinkage 3% and relaxation 2%, each as a percentage of P0. Find the total loss and the effective prestress.
steps: List the percentage losses: friction 4%, anchorage slip 3%, elastic shortening 2%, creep 6%, shrinkage 3%, relaxation 2%.
Add the percentages: 4 + 3 + 2 + 6 + 3 + 2 = 20%. This assumes each loss is a percentage of P0 and losses are added directly.
Effective prestress P_eff = P0 − ΔP = 1000 − 200 = 800 kN.
examples.answer: Total loss is 20% or 200 kN; effective prestress is 800 kN.
examples.check:
P0 = 1000.0
losses_percent = [4.0, 3.0, 2.0, 6.0, 3.0, 2.0]
total_percent = sum(losses_percent)
loss_kN = P0 * total_percent / 100.0
effective_kN = P0 - loss_kN
print(total_percent)
print(loss_kN)
print(effective_kN)

traps: Adding percentages of P0 is a preliminary estimate. Real losses interact; do not present the sum as exact.
Using degrees in the friction term μα. Convert to radians: 1° = π/180 rad.
Swapping creep and relaxation. Creep is concrete shortening; relaxation is steel stress loss at constant strain.
Using P0 in service stress checks. Use P_eff after all losses.
Forgetting that anchorage slip loss depends on tendon length L; a short tendon loses more stress for the same slip.

quiz.q: Name the three immediate losses of prestress.
quiz.a: Elastic shortening, friction and anchorage slip.

quiz.q: Why is elastic shortening loss small in a post-tensioned member when all tendons are jacked at the same time?
quiz.a: The concrete shortens during jacking, but the jack maintains force; there is little relative shortening after transfer. Loss is significant when tendons are stressed one by one because earlier tendons shorten when later ones compress the concrete.

quiz.q: A beam is jacked to P0 = 1200 kN. Take friction 5%, anchorage slip 2%, elastic shortening 3%, creep 4%, shrinkage 2% and relaxation 2% of P0. Find total loss and effective prestress.
A 30 m tendon and a 10 m tendon have the same jacking force. Both have the same curvature coefficient and wobble coefficient. Explain why the 30 m tendon has larger friction loss.
quiz.a: The exponent μα + kx grows with x. The longer tendon has more accumulated angle and more wobble length, so P_x/P0 is smaller and loss is larger.

quiz.q: Write the friction formula for P_x.
What is the difference between creep and relaxation?
quiz.a: Creep is time-dependent shortening of concrete under sustained stress. Relaxation is time-dependent loss of stress in steel held at constant strain.

quiz.q: Anchorage slip δ = 2 mm, tendon length L = 20 m, E_s = 195000 N/mm². Find the stress loss due to slip.
Why is it wrong to add all losses as percentages of P0 for final design?
quiz.a: Losses are not independent. Friction changes the force along the tendon, elastic shortening depends on concrete stress, and creep and shrinkage develop together. A final design computes each loss from the actual stress history and code model.

beyond: Not for the exam. Long-term loss monitoring uses load cells and vibrating-wire strain gauges on bridges. Modern low-relaxation strands and better grouts reduce time-dependent losses. The same ideas appear in creep and shrinkage models of codes and in finite-element time-step analysis. Search next for prestress loss monitoring and creep and shrinkage prediction.
